extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of ancient philosophy (readers of Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: A close-excerpt from Plato's Republic (Books I–II) presenting a dialogical examination of justice, injustice, the role of rulers, and the nature of the soul. Useful for studying Platonic arguments, thought experiments (e.g., Gyges' ring), and teleological accounts of function and excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruler's art aims at subjects' good
rubrics_metrics.description: The art of the ruler, considered as ruler, concerns only the good of his flock or subjects; rulers should provide for the best of their subjects rather than their own advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument contrasts ruling with other arts (medicine, navigation): just as a physician promotes patients' health, the true ruler's function is the good of those he rules; payment or compulsion is needed to induce good men to rule because they do not seek personal gain or honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct arts have distinct ends and excellences
rubrics_metrics.description: Each art has a separate function (end) which it fulfils best by its own proper excellence; an organ or craft fails its end when deprived of its excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: eye's end is seeing; pruning-hook best for pruning; medicine gives health; navigation gives safety at sea. This teleology underpins later claims about the soul and justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice is the excellence of the soul; injustice its defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is identified as the excellence (virtue/wisdom) of the soul; injustice is a defect or ignorance of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From this identification follows the inference that a just soul will live well and be happy, whereas an unjust soul will live ill and be miserable.

rubrics_metrics.name: The just life is happier than the unjust life
rubrics_metrics.description: Because justice is the soul's excellence, the just man and soul will live well and be blessed/happy; the unjust man, having an evil soul, will live ill and be unhappy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is argued via the teleological account of function/excellence for soul and by showing that injustice undermines unity and effective action, making it ultimately disadvantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injustice undermines cohesion and collective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Injustice creates divisions, hatreds, and fighting wherever it exists, rendering bodies (states, armies, families) incapable of united action; perfectly unjust groups could not act together unless they retained some justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue that apparent strength of injustice is illusory because injustice prevents the mutual cooperation necessary for successful collective enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good rulers do not seek payment or honour; may require compulsion
rubrics_metrics.description: Truly good men are ashamed to govern for pay or honour; therefore, to secure their service they must be induced by either payment, honour, or by a 'penalty' (necessity/fear) to take office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explanatory criterion about incentives and political practice: money and honour do not attract the best men, so necessity or obligation compels them to rule for the common good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins of justice as social compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Common account: justice arises as a mean or compromise between the best (doing injustice without being punished) and the worst (suffering injustice without the power of retaliation); law arises to prevent mutual harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Glaucon's reconstruction of the conventional origin of justice: people accept laws and mutual covenants because they cannot reliably secure the good of unpunished injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gyges' ring thought experiment (motivation for justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person could act unjustly with impunity (e.g., being invisible like Gyges), no one would remain just; thus, Glaucon argues people practice justice out of fear and necessity, not because they value it intrinsically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a psychological/evaluative test for whether justice is intrinsically valued: the claim is that behavior under absolute impunity reveals true motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of goods (intrinsic, mixed, instrumental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Threefold classification: (1) goods welcome for their own sakes (purely intrinsic), (2) goods desirable both in themselves and for their results (mixed), and (3) goods pursued only for their consequences (instrumental); question is which class justice belongs to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socrates places justice among the highest class (intrinsic + results), while the many view it as instrumental or a necessary evil; this classification frames the argument about justice's value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral criterion: just vs unjust desires
rubrics_metrics.description: The just person does not desire more than his like but desires more than his unlike; the unjust person desires more than both his like and unlike—i.e., the unjust seeks excess over everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show that the just are akin to the wise/good (who seek appropriate aims), whereas the unjust resemble the ignorant/bad in their excessive striving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful injustice aims to appear just
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest form of injustice is to be perfectly unjust in action while being reputed as just; the perfectly unjust man seeks to be deemed just while practicing injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glaucon instructs that when imagining the perfectly unjust man, we must allow him to have the reputation of justice—this defines the 'best' unjust life for comparative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument by function: soul's proper activities determine flourishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as each craft/organ's excellence secures its end, the soul's excellence (justice) enables it to perform its proper activities (deliberation, command), and only with that excellence will the soul fulfil its end (life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This teleological move is the backbone of the claim that justice causes flourishing: deprivation of excellence prevents fulfilment of the soul's ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thrasymachus' opposing claim: justice as advantage of the stronger
rubrics_metrics.description: Thrasymachus asserts that justice is the interest of the stronger (rulers) and that injustice, when practiced on a sufficient scale, is more profitable and advantageous than justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue treats this as a thesis to be refuted; it functions as a foil to develop definitions and counterarguments about justice's nature and value.
